title: Orchestrated throttling and safe-retry handshake for cross-region calls
creator: Aisha Rao
description:
Problem: Services across regions currently implement ad-hoc retry/backoff logic and idempotency semantics. During partial outages or overload events we see thundering herd behavior, circuit breaker flapping, and inconsistent cross-region failovers that violate SLOs.

Goal: Define and implement a lightweight client-runtime handshake and an orchestrated throttling model that standardizes safe retry semantics, short-lived idempotency tokens, hedged request behavior, and coordinated load-shedding for multi-region failover. This ticket covers the spec, SDK surface changes, runtime admit-controller prototype, and integration tests.

Scope: - Client SDK change to request a short-lived safe-retry token (SRT) before issuing hedged/parallel attempts for non-idempotent operations. - Runtime API and admit-controller that issues SRTs with attached backoff profile and quota metadata. - Standard backoff profiles (low-latency, throughput-optimized, conservative) and mapping by route/SLO. - Circuit-breaker propagation signals and a soft-fallback handshake for cross-region routing. - Load-shedding modes: rate-limit, priority-drop, and graceful-429 with Retry-After informed by admit-controller.

Out of scope: full enterprise idempotency coordination across databases, long-term idempotency stores, protocol-level encryption changes.
acceptance_criteria: SDKs can obtain an SRT and include it in hedged requests; runtime validates and rejects requests without valid SRT
Admit-controller issues backoff profile and per-client quota; runtime enforces per-route admission and emits metrics
End-to-end integration test simulates region partial outage and demonstrates stable failover with <= 2x p95 latency and no traffic spikes to recovering region
Circuit-breaker state is propagated to routing plane; failover occurs only when routing policy permits and respects client backoff profile
Documentation and migration guide for customers and platform teams are published
Canary rollout to 10% of traffic with automatic rollback on regression metric (increased error-rate or latency beyond SLO)
decisions: Use short-lived SRTs (60s default TTL) instead of long-lived idempotency tokens to avoid coordination and state churn
Adopt three canonical backoff profiles instead of infinite customization to simplify telemetry and quota accounting
Hedged requests allowed only when SRT present; otherwise SDK must fall back to sequential retry
Admit-controller will emit both admit/deny and suggested Retry-After header to enable graceful client backoff
tradeoffs: SRTs introduce a small extra RTT for obtaining tokens but reduce overall load amplification during failover
Restricting hedging to SRT holders reduces accidental fanout but requires SDK adoption effort
Choosing fixed profiles simplifies operations but may not be optimal for every bespoke workload
test_plan: Unit tests for SDK SRT acquisition and header propagation; integration test harness that spins up two simulated regions, triggers controlled overload in primary, verifies no spike in retry traffic, asserts that admit-controller metrics reflect correct denies/admits; chaos test to flip circuit-breakers and validate routing behavior.
rollout_plan: Feature-flag runtime admit-controller in staging and run synthetic workloads for 72h
Canary rollout to internal teams and 1% production traffic for 24h
Gradually increase to 10% with metric monitors and automatic rollback on SLO regressions
Full rollout after 2 weeks of stable canary and engineering signoff
implementation_notes: Runtime will expose /srt endpoint that validates client identity and returns token + profile metadata
SDKs add SRT cache per route with TTL refresh and jittered backoff for refresh attempts
Admit-controller integrates with existing quota service for per-customer burst accounting
Routing plane will accept circuit-breaker metadata via x-redwood-cb header to inform regional failover decisions
migration_guidance: Start with conservative profile for customer-facing routes. Platform teams should enable the SDK opt-in flag to test in their services. For services that cannot adopt SDK changes immediately, runtime will support legacy sequential retry with strict rate-limits until migration completes.
